title: Work queue or event log: the first question
summary: Before naming a product, decide the shape: a queue that deletes work when it is done, or a log that keeps events for many readers.

steps.title: Two shapes
body: Most "RabbitMQ or Kafka?" debates are really "queue or log?". Decide that first.
```text
WORK QUEUE  (RabbitMQ classic / quorum queue, Amazon SQS, Azure Service Bus queue)
producer ─► [ m5 m4 m3 m2 m1 ] ─► worker A  (m1, unacked)
─► worker B  (m2, unacked)
─► worker C  (m3, unacked)
ack m1 → m1 is DELETED.  Any free worker takes the next message.
One slow job holds up one worker, not the queue.  Retry and dead-letter per message.
EVENT LOG  (Kafka topic, Azure Event Hubs, Amazon Kinesis, RabbitMQ stream)
P0 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |   ◄─ group billing at offset 4
◄─ group search  at offset 1   (every group reads everything)
P1 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |           ◄─ billing at 3, search at 0
Nothing is deleted on read; retention (time, size) or compaction decides.
Order and parallelism are per partition: one consumer per partition per group.
- Queue: **tasks** ("resize this image"), done once by someone, then forgotten.
- Log: **facts** ("order 7 was placed"), kept, read by many, replayable.
> **See it:** open **Labs → Messaging builder → RabbitMQ** and play *Drain the backlog*, then
> **Labs → Messaging builder → Kafka** and play *More consumers than partitions*.

steps.prompt: Queue or log? Sort each requirement by the shape it needs.
items: Resize 10,000 uploaded images; each job done once by any worker
Build a new search index from the last 30 days of product changes
Five teams each want every order event, at their own pace
A job takes 20 minutes and must be retried on its own if it fails
Retry an email in 30 seconds, then park it after 5 attempts
One million clickstream events per second, kept for 7 days
explain: Replay, many independent readers and long retention point to a log. Individual retries, long jobs and "done means
gone" point to a queue. Plenty of systems need both, and that is fine: two workloads, two shapes.

steps.prompt: The `pdf-render` team put render jobs on a Kafka topic with 6 partitions. Most jobs take a second, some take 10 minutes. Small jobs now wait up to 12 minutes, adding pods beyond 6 changes nothing, and the logs show frequent rebalances. Why?
options: A slow record blocks every record behind it in its partition, parallelism is capped at 6 per group, and a 10-minute job exceeds `max.poll.interval.ms` (5 minutes by default), so the consumer is kicked out and the partition rebalances
Kafka is too slow for PDF rendering
The consumer should commit more often
explain: Kafka commits an **offset**, not individual messages, so a partition is processed in order: one slow job is
head-of-line blocking for everything behind it. That is the "Kafka as a task queue" anti-pattern; a work queue
(RabbitMQ, SQS, Service Bus) lets any free worker take the next job.

steps.title: The decision criteria
body: Ask these in a design review, in roughly this order:
1. **Work queue or event stream?** Tasks done once, or facts kept for many readers.
2. **Replay?** Will anyone need to re-read last week (a new service, a bug fix, a backfill)? That needs a log.
3. **Fan-out count.** Two subscribers is easy anywhere; twenty independent teams is what logs are built for.
4. **Ordering.** Usually per entity (per order, per account), never global. Kafka: per partition, by key. Queues:
per queue with one consumer, or Service Bus sessions, SQS FIFO message groups.
5. **Throughput and retention.** Thousands per second for minutes, or hundreds of thousands per second for weeks.
6. **Routing flexibility.** RabbitMQ exchanges route on keys and headers; a log routes by topic and key only.
7. **Ops burden.** Who patches, monitors and upgrades it at 3 a.m.? A managed service moves that cost to the bill.
8. **Team skills.** The broker the team already runs well beats a theoretically better one nobody knows.
9. **Cost.** Instance hours and disks, or per-request and per-throughput-unit cloud pricing.
The lines are blurring, carefully: **RabbitMQ streams** (a log type in RabbitMQ, with offsets and retention) give
RabbitMQ shops replay, and Kafka **share groups** (KIP-932, "queues for Kafka") add per-record acknowledgement and
more consumers than partitions. Share groups were a preview in Kafka 4.1 and are production-ready since **Kafka 4.2**
(4.2.1 fixes a share-group deadlock). Client support lags the broker, so check that your client (Confluent.Kafka
follows librdkafka) supports share consumers before you design around them.

steps.prompt: Match each term to what it means for the design.
pairs: Tells a queue the message can be deleted
A group's position in a partition; rewind it to replay
How long a log keeps records, read or not
Any free worker takes the next message from one queue
Consumers sharing a topic's partitions; each group gets every record
Keeps only the latest record per key
explain: If a requirement is phrased in the right-hand language ("rewind", "every team gets every record", "latest value per
key"), you have found your shape.

steps.prompt: A 12,000-message backlog, 50 ms per message, 8 workers. What does this print?
code: int kafkaWorkers = Math.Min(workers, partitions);     // one consumer per partition per group
Console.WriteLine(backlog * msPerMessage / kafkaWorkers / 1000);   // seconds to drain with Kafka
Console.WriteLine(backlog * msPerMessage / workers / 1000);        // seconds with competing consumers on a queue
explain: With 4 partitions only 4 of the 8 workers get work, so the topic drains in 150 s; a queue uses all 8 and drains in
75 s. More partitions fix it for Kafka, but adding partitions later changes which partition each key maps to, so size

steps.prompt: The team scaled `render` from 6 to 10 pods and throughput did not move. What does this output tell you?
options: The topic has 6 partitions: the group gives each partition to one member, so 4 pods have nothing assigned and sit idle
4 pods failed to connect to the broker
The group is rebalancing and will spread the load in a minute
The 4 pods are standby replicas that take over writes
explain: `#PARTITIONS 0` is the tell. Within one group a partition has exactly one owner (with the classic protocol and with
the newer `group.protocol=consumer`, KIP-848, alike). Fix it with more partitions, planned with the key mapping in
mind, or by moving this workload to a queue.

steps.title: Queue or log, with reasons
prompt: Turn the first question into code a design-review bot can run. The tests define
record Req(bool Replay, int Subscribers, int RetentionDays, bool PerMessageRetry, bool LongJobs, bool Routing);
Write `(string Shape, List<string> Reasons) Classify(Req r)`.
**Log reasons**, in this order: `Replay` → `"replay needs a log"`; `Subscribers >= 3` → `"{n} independent subscribers"`;
**Queue reasons**, in this order: `PerMessageRetry` → `"per-message retry and dead-lettering"`; `LongJobs` →
`"long jobs would block a partition"`; `Routing` → `"routing by key or header"`.
- more log reasons → `("log", log reasons)`; more queue reasons → `("queue", queue reasons)`;
- a tie with at least one reason → `("either", log reasons then queue reasons)`;
- no reasons at all → `("either", ["no strong signal: pick what the team runs well"])`.
solution: if (r.LongJobs) queue.Add("long jobs would block a partition");
if (r.Routing) queue.Add("routing by key or header");
if (log.Count == 0) return ("either", new List<string> { "no strong signal: pick what the team runs well" });
hints: Build two lists with `if` statements, then compare their counts.
template: var dojoA = Classify(new Req(Replay: true, Subscribers: 5, RetentionDays: 30, PerMessageRetry: false, LongJobs: false, Routing: false));
Dojo.Eq("clickstream: reasons", new List<string> { "replay needs a log", "5 independent subscribers", "keeps data 30 days" }, dojoA.Reasons);
var dojoB = Classify(new Req(false, 1, 0, true, true, false));
Dojo.Eq("render jobs: reasons", new List<string> { "per-message retry and dead-lettering", "long jobs would block a partition" }, dojoB.Reasons);
var dojoC = Classify(new Req(true, 2, 1, false, false, true));
Dojo.Eq("one each: log reasons first", new List<string> { "replay needs a log", "routing by key or header" }, dojoC.Reasons);
var dojoD = Classify(new Req(false, 2, 1, false, false, false));
Dojo.Eq("nothing stands out: the advice", new List<string> { "no strong signal: pick what the team runs well" }, dojoD.Reasons);
Dojo.Eq("3 subscribers is the threshold", "log", Classify(new Req(false, 3, 0, false, false, false)).Shape);
record Req(bool Replay, int Subscribers, int RetentionDays, bool PerMessageRetry, bool LongJobs, bool Routing);
